articles.title: How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base
articles.summary: With ia.i, a conversational interface, and the IARA governance platform, Itaú is applying its AI First strategy to customers and employees — in one of Brazil’s most regulated sectors.
articles.content:
Title: How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/itau-generative-ai

Markdown Content:
## The challenge is to make the technology disappear

Creating a close, personalized experience for millions of customers in a country like Brazil is, first and foremost, a question of simplicity rather than of models.

“Much of it is about making something simple, direct, and useful, delivering a direct benefit to the customer, and making the technology almost unnoticeable,” says Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO of Itaú.

The standard he describes is demanding: the solution must solve a real everyday problem and be direct, simple, and memorable. Technology serves as the means, never as the centerpiece of the experience.

There is demand for this. A study by Itaú in partnership with Grupo Consumoteca shows that 80% of Brazilians want to better organize their financial lives and seek more effective support for decisions, and that 65% would like technologies that act as a financial copilot, providing ongoing guidance.

> “OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## ia.i: from convenience to advice, in one place

The journey began in 2024, when the bank introduced the first Inteligência Itaú capabilities for specific financial needs. ia.i is the next stage: a complete conversational layer, activated by text or voice, bringing interactions related to checking accounts, credit, cards, insurance, and other services into one environment — and connecting customers to specialized human support whenever needed.

This breadth was precisely what guided the choice of models.

“OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions,” Mazzei explains. “From the simplest ones, which need to be efficient in cost and latency, to more complex solutions, where reasoning and all the necessary grounding are required to provide an appropriate answer.”

Having a range of models — rather than a single model — made it possible to deliver the complete solution in one product. At the center of this experience is Customer DNA, a layer of financial context that helps the bank understand the needs, habits, and life stages of approximately 70 million customers. Under governance and responsible AI controls, GPT models are among the components that help maintain and enrich this representation, making interactions progressively more relevant.

The solution rests on three principles: interactivity, multimodality — text, voice, image, and clicks in the same experience — and individualization.

With approximately 300,000 customers in the first phase, the bank entered a period of learning about the real relationship between customer and product.

“We can understand how customers begin to use this product more deeply and see how it can directly benefit each person’s daily financial life,” says Mazzei. Its presence extends across the journey: from a question about an expense in an account statement to investment advice and convenient transactions on WhatsApp.

> “The financial world often has products that are not so straightforward and need this context, this simpler relationship with money.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## IARA: the layer that makes scale possible

Behind the visible experiences is an architectural decision. To operate AI at the scale of a bank, Itaú built IARA — a governance and orchestration platform that gives teams controlled access to different models in line with internal policies. OpenAI is among the model providers available in this environment.

This layer supports solutions such as the legal department’s, where the platform automates document reading, analysis, and interpretation. The solution operates on a repository of more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80% in stages of the department’s processes.

“It is essential that this information be preserved, remain within the bank’s context, and access models in a secure, governed way, with an understanding of token-use efficiency so that the entire solution is economically viable for the bank,” Mazzei says.

IARA addresses three problems at once: cost control per token, accuracy of responses, and application of responsible AI policies. In such a regulated sector, this makes it possible to move quickly while maintaining control.

“When we talk about Responsible AI at the bank, it is a discipline we take great care with,” he says. “We need customers to interact with the bank and our responses to align with our values and culture.” This includes reducing any risk of bias that may arise in frontier models.

Responsible AI principles guide the entire lifecycle of solutions, from development to continuous monitoring, aiming to ensure safety, transparency, ethics, and regulatory compliance as the technology scales.

> “IARA is a fundamental platform, because it ensures we can have governance and observability in a highly regulated environment.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## AI First on the inside, too

The bank’s AI First strategy extends beyond end customers. The same intelligence layer that supports ia.i also assists specialists, managers, and customer service teams.

Mazzei describes a range extending from automating simple tasks to performing work that was previously unfeasible — but adds value to customer relationships: summaries before meetings, meeting preparation, understanding a specific issue, and developing plans and alternatives that were previously less obvious and time-consuming.

The bank has significant expectations for this implementation: three times more time available for customer relationships, service up to twice as fast, and conversations up to three times more effective.

> “This set of tools in the hands of relationship managers allows us to focus on what matters most: creating value for our customers.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

## Results overview

*   ia.i reached approximately 300,000 customers in its first phase, covering everything from convenient transactions to investment advice, activated by text or voice.

*   The IARA platform makes different models available to the bank’s teams with governance, observability, cost control per token, and enforcement of Responsible AI.

*   The legal solution operates on more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80%.

*   Using a range of models made it possible to serve both cost- and latency-sensitive cases and those requiring deeper reasoning; GPT‑5.x models are part of Customer DNA, which provides financial context for approximately 70 million customers.

## Lessons for leaders

*   Measure the experience by its simplicity, rather than sophistication. The goal is for the technology to go unnoticed and the benefit to be apparent.

*   Choose a range of models, rather than a single one. Real journeys combine low-latency interactions with decisions that require reasoning.

*   Build the governance layer before scaling. Observability, cost control, and responsible AI make scale viable in regulated sectors.

*   Treat bias and cultural alignment as product requirements. Responses to customers must reflect the institution’s values.

*   Apply the strategy internally, too. Giving time back to teams frees up human relationships where they matter most.

## Tips

*   Start with concrete everyday problems, such as a question about an account statement or a simple transaction.

*   Launch to an initial customer group and use it to learn actual behavior before expanding.

*   Centralize model access on one platform to maintain control over costs and quality.

*   Monitor token efficiency from day one — economic viability is part of the design.

*   Combine conversation and navigation: not every action is best handled through natural language.

## Next steps

ia.i continues to evolve. The bank expects to make the experience available to its entire customer base by the end of 2026. Planned capabilities for the next stages include product simulations and sign-ups, as well as recurring financial analyses of income, expenses, and habits.

For Mazzei, the significance of the initiative goes beyond the product — the bank has navigated decades of transformation, with customers’ habits and expectations constantly changing.

> “Leading the AI era is about responding faster to our customers’ needs. It is about understanding how technology can add value and help customers engage with financial products and services in a much simpler, more direct way that helps them achieve what they are seeking.”

—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

articles.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
articles.summary: Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.
articles.content:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at
TechCrunch Disrupt
.
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit
announced
a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.
“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”
Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have
helped
the company grow its revenue significantly.
Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.
There is evidence on
the company’s website
, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a
blog post
in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees
posted
on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.
TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back.
Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.
“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”
Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.
“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”
This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models.

articles.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
articles.summary: The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles.
articles.content:
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency
said
Thursday.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.”
The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”
This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and
hacked French company Hugging Face
— kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI
apologized to Australia
after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.
At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.
Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found
no evidence
its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.
CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.
For now, the closest parallel seems to be
Anthropic’s July disclosure
of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.
In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

articles.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
articles.summary: According to Elorian's evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
articles.content:
Elorian
, the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.
The model,
Glimpse
, is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface is waitlist-only, so for now it’s a results table and a thesis. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see.
Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.
For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night.
Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”
“Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said.
The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against.
Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.
But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.
The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test.

articles.title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
articles.summary: The data comes from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.
articles.content:
Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.
Vercel data
published on Thursday
shows that, within two weeks of its launch,
the buzzy decision model
was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.
Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from
OpenAI
and
Amazon
, among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.
The data comes from Vercel’s
AI gateway
, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.
The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend.
While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be
complementary rather than competitive
.

articles.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
articles.summary: Actor and angel investor Mark Wahlberg says he's OK with using AI in filmmaking, provided it's used "to enhance what you're doing."
articles.content:
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.
Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.
“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”
That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.
Image Credits:
Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch
“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”
When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the
CAA Vault
, a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.
“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.
“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”

articles.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
articles.summary: Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes, known as "superfakes," as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
articles.content:
Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “
superfakes
,” as genuine items. A startup called
Veritas
wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.
Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link.
“Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.
The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass.
“The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.”
This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.
Image Credits:
Veritas x ATHLOS
The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.
The company has so far
raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding
led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.
Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.
Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced
Thursday afternoon
.

articles.title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
articles.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad envisions a future of “self-driving companies,” where AI agents handle day-to-day tasks and people focus on higher-level decisions.
articles.content:
Replit
CEO and co-founder
Amjad Masad
has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.
He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste.
“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.
He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.
“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”
Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.
And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.
“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.
The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.
“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”
He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.)
“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
Nvidia’s new Arm-based laptop chip is an exciting new challenger, but exclusively for the high-end.﻿

Nvidia’s new SoC is available in Windows laptops from six different manufacturers. We’ve collectively tested four of them so far.
|  Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge
Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models.
The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own
Tom Warren fully reviewed
. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing.
All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a
Surface Laptop Ultra
or a smaller
Asus ProArt P14
with 24GB of RAM.
These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s
a lot
to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week.
Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep?
Does it just work?
A laptop costing $7,000 better just work, and work well.
Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge
Antonio Di Benedetto:
Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer.
Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities.
Sean Hollister:
Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode.
But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below.
Tom Warren:
I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming.
Can it game?
Gears of War: E-Day
running on the Surface Laptop Ultra during a Microsoft demo.
Photo: Meron Menghistab
TW:
Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games.
I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run
Black Myth: Wukong
at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in
Cyberpunk 2077
and averaged 66fps, and
Forza Horizon 6
managed an average of 57fps.
In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.
SH:
Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in
Returnal
(at 1440p with high settings),
Expedition 33
(at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings),
Jedi Survivor
(DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and
Shadow of the Tomb Raider
(at native 1800p and highest spec).
But when I fired up
Helldivers 2
, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up.
Star Wars Zero Company
is even more
CPU-bound
—
the Spark didn’t care whether I was maximizing or minimizing the graphics and screen resolution. No matter what I tried, I typically saw my framerate capped between 37fps and 39fps in battle.
Even ancient and low-powered games can have quirks. I tried the 2003 title
Max Payne 2
and saw situations where framerate dipped to 50fps. I even saw a few hitches in the excellent
UFO 50
, a collection of 2D games, though a couple other 2D games ran great.
I’m also not sure if RTX Spark is suitable for VR yet. The
excellent
Titanfall 2
VR mod
worked, and it seemed to run fine at first, but lost a little stability after a few minutes. That could be my Wi-Fi, because the driver for Valve’s
Steam Frame
wireless adapter wouldn’t install on the Spark. Neither did Steam’s streaming audio solution, so the audio came out of the Nvidia laptop instead of the headset.
Just so we’re clear, all of this is assuming you want a laptop maxing out its fans and positively dumping heat on your desk or lap. That’s not unusual for thin gaming notebooks, but it’s
way
louder and hotter than a good desktop or handheld.

I’ve wanted a MacBook Pro-like laptop with full PC gaming chops for as long as I can remember, so I was hyped for these laptops to deliver the goods in graphics. The first night, I set up the Asus ProArt P16, with all 128GB of its ridiculously large pool of memory, and when I booted up

for my planned online evening with some friends my first thought was, “Well, that looks okay. I guess.” I know
Big Walk
isn’t some triple-A graphical titan, but it has some fairly demanding graphics for the “
friend slop
” genre. I expected the N1X to max it out, or at least get close, but not really.
I had to bump the P16’s 4K display down to 2560 x 1600, and instead of
Big Walk’s
Highest or Very high graphics presets, I brought it down to High to maintain a decently solid 60-ish fps. Does any of that really matter for this silly co-op game about solving puzzles with your buddies? Of course not. It looked fine, after all. But it was a sobering reminder that this “superchip” is no graphical magician.
As Tom and Sean point out, RTX Spark can do some decent gaming, but temper your expectations for medium or even low settings in some cases, and be ready to rely on DLSS and frame gen. There’s no denying that cheaper desktops and even laptops with discrete Nvidia graphics cards can easily beat out an N1X. Nvidia claims it’s like having an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU in an SoC, but in my testing it was somewhere between that and an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU — not a slouch, for sure, but if you’re a gamer first your money goes much further with traditional Nvidia graphics cards.
How’s the battery life?
Sadly, only Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra has that slick magnetic USB-C charging.
Photo: Meron Menghistab
SH:
Nvidia’s partners saw fit to equip their first wave of RTX Spark laptops with some of the biggest batteries you can bring on an airplane with no questions asked — but even with a 99.9 watt-hour pack like the one in my Asus ProArt P16, these laptops won’t be winning awards for longevity. While Tom and Antonio spent their days testing every use case under the sun, I made the P16 my daily driver for
normal
work while watching the battery meter like a hawk. That mostly means writing stories in a web browser, and it’s not quite lasting the day.
My best run was 5 hours and 40 minutes of real-world work at 50 percent brightness, including an hour-long video call with Tom and Antonio to strategize our RTX Spark coverage plan. The next day, I got only about 5 hours from a full charge because I spent two of them
editing this video
in Capcut. The third time I drained the battery, it took 5 hours, too.
With web work, I’m typically seeing 13-17 watt battery drain on the laptop’s default settings, but that climbs to 20-30 watts with light video work, up to 50 watts during the (brief) Capcut video export, and I made it jump all the way to 120 watts playing
Indiana Jones and the Great Circle
. The battery couldn’t keep feeding at that rate — it slowly went down, and at 30 percent charge I saw a big performance hit as it dropped dramatically to 60 watts.
The good news is the Asus charges
fast
from a 140W USB-C PD power source. It took 20 minutes to go from dead to 50 percent battery, another 15 minutes to get to 70 percent, and a total of 1 hour, 15 minutes to reach 95 percent charge.
AD:
I’ve had to run lots of benchmarks while plugged in, so I haven’t been able to spend as much time testing battery life as I’d normally like. Anecdotally, in lots of fits and starts, battery life seems solid. As Sean saw, you’re unlikely to get through a full eight hour work day unless you’re going out of your way to be efficient. And if you fire up anything heavy, like a local AI model (more on that in a minute), you won’t even make it to lunch. I’ll eventually do more thoroug

Tech

Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free
The new policy allows Meta to crawl all websites ‘associated’ with a business account.
The new policy allows Meta to crawl all websites ‘associated’ with a business account.
by
Emma Roth
Oct 16, 2026, 2:02 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge
Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Meta’s new terms appear to give it permission to crawl and scrape websites “associated” with the businesses that use its platforms — including online publishers, according to
a report from
Nieman Lab
. The
new terms
, which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products.
While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell
Nieman Lab
that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like
a site’s robots.txt file
. That could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers.
The new policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger:
You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
Roberts pushes back on
Nieman Lab
’s reporting, saying “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false… Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation.” Meta has followed
OpenAI
in
striking AI licensing deals with CNN
, Fox News,
USA Today
, and People Inc., but these terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content.
“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, tells
Nieman Lab
.
Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications,
writes in a post on X
that this change isn’t meant to target news sites. “This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites.”
Businesses that don’t agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes,” the terms say. Last month, Meta
launched a new Meta One subscription
that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. “Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free,”
Nieman Lab
says.

Added a statement from Meta and legal commentary.

The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.

Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.

articles.content:
More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones.
The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors
convert light into electricity,
bipolar cells
process that signal, and
ganglion cells
transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN
Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.'s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN
CAPTURE
Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing
camera
capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a
fiber-optic cable
.
CONVERT
A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN
DISPLAY
A laser
projector
on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of
near-infrared light
directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the
pupil
and on to the
retinal implant
in the back of the eye.
SEE
The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an
electrode
and two
photovoltaic cells
, which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery.
Update
: This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats.
Linda Marsa is a former
Los Angeles Times
reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

articles.summary: I. Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to…
articles.content:
I. Meet cute
Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer.
When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress.
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly.
A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host.
“Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.”
“Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well,
I
can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the
Times
. And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.”
Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer.
For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring.
At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated.
“There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.”
Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point.
“St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.”
“I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.”
Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty.
“Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.”
II. How they came alive
Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly.
A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.”
Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought.
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.”
Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day.
Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues.
People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government.
Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. But votes from humans provided the greatest insight into “quality of life,” that oh-so-nebulous concept, and thus counted the most.
There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing.
(Other cities in the region operated differently, of course. Like Turnbull City, where instead of expecting residents to volunteer every stray notion, the City Core gathered information via ubiquitous surveillance. Cameras and Quill sniffers, tracking devices on vehicles—the things privacy laws in both Mainspring and St. Barnabas had banned. A city like Turnbull tracked its people to meet their needs without their needing to say anything.)
Sandi and Raeford, as two of the people who voted the most, were among the earliest to suspect their cities were developing minds of their own. At first the clues were subtle: Raeford voted about a hazardous sidewalk crack, and instantly the vote had an annotation mentioning the Argentine ant colony under the cement, the local rainfall patterns, and recent trends in skateboard design—much too soon to be the work of a human. Sandi had ideas about the communal compost station on her block, and the Mainspring City Core made subtle adjustments to her proposal.
And then it became obvious to anyone who was paying attention, around the same time in both cities. One day, the number of votes nearly doubled in both St. Barnabas and Mainspring. People voted on a birdfeeder or a public toilet only to see a second vote, pro or con, within a split second—but also, some votes from months or years earlier suddenly had new upvotes or downvotes.
“The city is voting!” Raeford wrote on the City Core message board in St. Barnabas.
There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing, opinions that came from seeing the big picture and understanding that a street closure in one place might mean a traffic nightmare elsewhere, with everyone trying to get to the big game.
Some residents saw this as a problem to be solved; others wanted to throw their cities a big coming-of-age party. A week later, though, almost everyone had gotten used to the idea that they had a new friend.
III. Thrown together
Ask most people in either city, and they’d say that St. Barnabas and Mainspring weren’t quite rivals—but they certainly had some friendly competition. Before the dispute over the annual meeting of the World Geographical Society, they’d also vied for the same football team and major-league baseball team. St. Barnabas had pushed to have the Mainspring airport built close enough to serve both cities, but in the end St. Barnabas had ended up with its own small, dilapidated airfield.
The real static between them had to do with vibes. Mainspring was too buttoned-up, too full of corporate offices: tech, health care, publishing, transportation. St. Barnabas would be nothing without its three universities and all the cultural enterprises that had sprung up around them—not to mention the small biotech firms and other tech ventures near the campuses. People in Mainspring thought St. Barnabas was full of flakes; in St. Barnabas they referred to Mainspring as the Straitlaced City (and in the next breath, they’d add that at least it wasn’t Turnbull).
Both City Cores were shaped by the votes of their humans, so of course they absorbed all the prejudices and attitudes of everyone who lived within their city limits. But also, Barnabas and Mainspring simply … got on each other’s nerves.
After the geographer thing, Mainspring and Barnabas avoided communicating as much as possible. Some contact was unavoidable—like, they shared information about some nasty weather, and they both drew water from the Temple River. The two cities were close enough for people to go back and forth, and a few even commuted.
But for the most part, the two cities could ignore each other.
Until they couldn’t.
A new generation of leaders took office in both places, with words like “intercity cooperation” constantly on their lips. A high-speed rail line could shorten the trip between Mainspring and St. Barnabas to around 23 minutes, and the two cities could also pool more real-time information about the sudden weather events that kept happening. They could become a Regional Center of Excellence, whatever
that
meant, combining the innovations from Barnabas’s labs with Mainspring’s expertise in technical implementation. They could work together to attract tourism, conventions, sporting events, dreamleases, and all the other stuff they’d always competed for.
“It’s preposterous,” Mainspring complained to Turnbull. “I’m going to be saddled with a ridiculous partner who doesn’t even know their own mind. St. Barnabas will be the death of me.”
“I hope your human leaders come to their senses,” Turnbull said. “Or you can find a way to slow-walk this until they undoubtedly lose the next election. You’re a lovely city, and you have so much potential that mustn’t be squandered.”

articles.content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it.
What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.
There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?
There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is
trialing
one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are
testing dog drugs
that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like
obesity and osteoarthritis
, and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on
longevity medicines for
domesticated cats.
I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it.
That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though.
I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin.
Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?”
Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced.
Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of.
Alcor
, a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider.
With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero. Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated. As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.”
I miss Peppy. But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not.
RIP to the one and only Peppy.

articles.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
articles.summary: Social media bans are stacking up. articles.content:
Social media bans are stacking up. In July,
France
joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was
blocked
by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to
forbid kids under 16
from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the
EU
has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that
four in five teens under 16
made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from
using
a sibling’s face for ID to
drawing
fake facial hair.
Some proponents of bans have called for an
increased focus
on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age.
In our work
, we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.
Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world.
A less safe internet for kids
When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop
social skills
and refine their
identities
. Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.
It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year,
parents told us
that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon;
research
all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to
social media
as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.
When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if
unconventional
, platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or
podcast comment sections
. Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to
abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban,
preliminary research
shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents.
Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the
fewest eyes on the digital street
. Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them.
A less safe internet for all
Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.
Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.
Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now
blocked by a federal court
), and
Australia’s eSafety Commissioner
is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users,
particularly journalists
and
human rights defenders
working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation.
What could work instead?
Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the
incentives
that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.
For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by
limiting the collection and use of data
that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all
parents and teens we spoke with
want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want.
Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands.
Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use  digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business.
Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are.
Michal Luria
is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization's work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems.
Aliya Bhatia
is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms.
Danah Boyd
is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is
Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census
.

# ChatGPT becomes a full Chrome browser assistant that reads and acts on your open tabs

[Matthias Bastian](https://the-decoder.com/author/matthias-bastian/)[View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthias-bastian-128b71b1/ "View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian")

 Oct 16, 2026

**ChatGPT can now access open tabs right in the Chrome browser and take actions on them.** Users can target open tabs with `@chrome`, while Chat mode pulls data from several tabs at once. Work mode lets the tool control tabs through Computer Use to send messages, fill out forms, download files, or group tabs. [GPT-6 Astra is the best Computer Use model](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-astra-is-the-first-model-making-openai-willing-to-declare-the-agi-era/) on the market right now, and it can handle complex workflows with many steps.

Your full chat history now sits in the upgraded ChatGPT sidebar right next to the web page you're viewing. In OpenAI's [examples](https://x.com/ChatGPT/status/2110823741991354728), the extension compares products across open tabs by size, material, shipping time, and return rules, sums up articles in plain language, or matches up price pages from different sellers. The updated [Chrome extension](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/chatgpt/hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg) works with all ChatGPT plans.

Title: China plans to tighten export controls on open-weight models and 23 key AI technologies

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/china-plans-to-tighten-export-controls-on-open-weight-models-and-23-key-ai-technologies/

Published Time: 2026-10-16T17:42:47+00:00

Markdown Content:
**China's commerce and science ministries have released a draft update to the nation's list of banned and restricted export technologies.**

The catalog targets 23 key AI technologies across large models, agents, compute clusters, and data processing. AI tools that can write or alter malware on their own to attack critical infrastructure, the military, or government agencies face a total export ban. Certain AI tools for finding software vulnerabilities won't be banned outright, though they will face new export limits.

Large AI models also face export controls in two cases. The first covers models trained on China's "important data" (as defined by the country's Data Security Law and related rules) that offer services based on it. Lawfully public data is exempt. Tiny amounts of up to 0.1 percent are also allowed if the data was cleaned beforehand, never shows up in AI outputs, and doesn't substantially boost the model's R&D capacity for core tech in that field.

The second case covers the core technologies behind large models, including weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training or inference methods. These controls kick in once a model hits 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, has at least 2 trillion parameters, or ranks in the global top 10. Export officials determine that top-10 status using public rankings from major domestic and foreign evaluators or industry platforms, looking at overall performance, specific tasks, safety, or global usage numbers.

"This move does not mean 'China is shutting down open-weight models,' but it does indicate the Chinese government establishing the optionality to shut down future open-weight models at will," [writes Dean W. Ball](https://x.com/deanwball/status/2111150928997019765), head of strategic futures at OpenAI. Ball adds that Beijing's framework is a "mirror image" of the model-weight export controls the US government has already put in place.

This will likely push US companies that rely on open-weight AI to double down on domestic models instead of Chinese alternatives. Europe is in a much tougher spot. The EU has been banking on running open-weight models in domestic clouds to stay independent, alongside companies that want to host closed top-tier models on local servers. That sovereignty strategy falls apart when all the best open models come from the US or China and can get cut off by export controls at any time. At least AI tech that is already public through open-source releases or research papers skips these new rules entirely.

## Fast-track rules protect China's open-source boom while restricting local foreign deployments

To avoid choking off its domestic open-source boom, [China is introducing](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/zcfb/dwmygl/art/2026/art/61446ab4beee4f63973d4d0ab3097648.html) a fast-track process at the same time. Publishing restricted AI tech and weights as open source qualifies for "automatic licensing." The same goes for Chinese firms that run their own data centers abroad, tape out chips overseas, conduct research with foreign partners, or help set international standards. Under the ministry's rules, eligible exports are cleared the moment a company files the paperwork.

Using restricted models through API calls, apps, websites, SaaS tools, or lightweight versions on local devices stays free of these export controls. Installing restricted AI tech on local servers abroad, however, requires a standard export license. Companies can still use the streamlined process if the software runs on their own overseas cloud.

Beijing also pledges to back AI development in the Global South and ease exports for capacity building, tech sharing, and joint rulemaking within the [World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization](https://the-decoder.com/chinas-new-world-artificial-intelligence-cooperation-organization-is-president-xis-clearest-play-yet-for-a-parallel-ai-order/), a bloc China launched to counter Western AI bodies. Until the final rules take effect, companies must register affected exports through the commerce ministry's portal.
