Title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon is closer to the AI frontier than any Google model in months

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/googles-gemini-4-argon-is-closer-to-the-ai-frontier-than-any-google-model-in-months/

Published Time: 2026-10-16T15:03:46+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Google Deepmind is the second major AI lab to pass 95 percent on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark. But the results depend heavily on the testing method, and Argon trails rivals in math and software engineering, according to Epoch AI.**

Google Deepmind's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, scored 97.5 percent on ARC-AGI-3 at a cost of $4,800 using the "Provider Adapter Harness," a test setup that uses vendor-specific features like retained reasoning and context compaction. According to ARC Prize, Google is now the second AI lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark on what is widely considered the toughest benchmark for general problem-solving. Only GPT-6 Astra scores higher at 99.9 percent.

Across the 25 public games of ARC-AGI-3, Gemini 4 Argon (yellow) and GPT-6 Astra (blue) both needed 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline (purple) and often came close to the speedrun record (red). | Image: ARC Prize

Like Astra, Argon needed 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline across the 25 public games. It matched or beat the speedrun record in three games and came within 10 percent of the best time in six others. On older versions of the benchmark, Argon scored 91.3 percent on ARC-AGI-2 ($0.32 per task) and 98.5 percent on ARC-AGI-1 ($0.16 per task), based on the introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Across the 25 public games in ARC-AGI-3, Gemini 4 Argon (yellow) and GPT-6 Astra (blue) both required 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline (purple) and often came close to the speedrun record (red). | Image: ARC Prize

## Benchmark results depend heavily on the testing setup

In the "Standard Harness," which only allows simple notes between rounds, Argon drops to 49.8 percent at low reasoning for $5,800. This gap traces back to a July 2026 dispute when [OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol beat Claude Opus 5 on ARC-AGI-3 using two API settings](https://the-decoder.com/openai-claims-gpt-5-6-sol-beats-opus-5-on-arc-agi-3-with-its-latest-api-and-two-additional-settings/).

GPT-5.6 Sol only managed 7.8 percent in the standard environment, which discards internal reasoning after each action and used an older interface lacking newer Claude API features. That meant Claude was tested under different conditions than GPT-5.6. When tested with OpenAI's own Responses API, including "Retained Reasoning" and smart context "Compaction," the model jumped to 38.3 percent and beat Opus 5 at 30.2 percent. OpenAI argued that benchmarks always measure the technical environment too. ARC Prize co-founder Francois Chollet then allowed general, publicly available API settings.

API problems also prevented Argon from completing all 55 games in the Standard Harness, [according to the testers](https://x.com/arcprize/status/2110768292101042240). At low reasoning, the system finished 42 games (49.8 percent), at medium 46 games (46.3 percent). At the highest level, it only completed 19 games, so ARC Prize did not publish a score. The reported results still cover all 55 games by including partial points from aborted runs.

## Argon closes the gap but lags in math and coding

Research institute Epoch AI tracked Google's progress too. Argon [scored 165 points](https://x.com/EpochAIResearch/status/2110693857742717372) on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), tying Fable 5.1 and landing just behind Opus 5.5 (167) and GPT-6 Astra (166). The ECI combines over 50 benchmarks into a single capability scale, similar to how Artificial Analysis builds its main score.

With an ECI score of 165 points, Google is closer to the current AI frontier led by GPT-6 Astra (166) and Opus 5.5 (167) than it has been since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February 2026. | Image: Epoch AI

Argon jumps well ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (157 points) and brings Google closer to the top than at any point since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February. [Artificial Analysis and Vals.ai](https://the-decoder.com/google-gemini-4-argon-closes-the-gap-with-openai-and-anthropic-but-doesnt-take-a-clear-lead/) confirmed this trend before.

Performance varies by domain, though. According to [Epoch AI](https://x.com/EpochAIResearch/status/2110693870308925898), Argon leads several knowledge, agent, and vision benchmarks, but early estimates put it in eighth on the Math ECI and sixth on the Software Engineering Index (SWE ECI).

articles.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
articles.content:
Title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins

Published Time: 2026-10-16T17:02:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained._

_We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards._

_Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy._

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the [FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard](https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/fips/186-2/final/docs/fips186-2.pdf) which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was `SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90` with no information where it came from.

[Neal Koblitz](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~koblitz/) and [Alfred Menezes](https://uwaterloo.ca/scholar/ajmeneze) wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “[A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/1018.pdf)”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an [amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds](https://saweis.net/posts/nist-curve-seed-origins.html) and a [bounty for anyone who could find them](https://words.filippo.io/seeds-bounty/).

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

> _“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”_

> Jerry Solinas, 2015

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

## Claude found the seeds

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

**In under half an hour**, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s `lrand48` random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (**t**) for some number of iterations (**n**). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

## What this means

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

## How it was found

Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator [`lrand48`](https://linux.die.net/man/3/lrand48), which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.

The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the [Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra%E2%80%93Lenstra%E2%80%93Lov%C3%A1sz_lattice_basis_reduction_algorithm) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by [srand48](https://linux.die.net/man/3/srand48), with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.

However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.

Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:

> This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.

> Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.

## Claude found some base points too

But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?

While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3 and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in [FreeLIP](https://cr.yp.to/speed/mult/freelip.html), [Arjen Lenstra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjen_Lenstra)'s long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of [Victor Shoup](https://shoup.net/)'s [NTL library](https://libntl.org/) shipped the same code.

The recipe here is simple:

1.   Seed the generator with a small integer.
2.   Throw away seven outputs.
3.   Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.
4.   Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.

Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.

As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.

## Open questions

Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.

Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.

There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.

## The bounty

The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the [Internet Security Research Group](https://www.abetterinternet.org/).

## Who we are

This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.

## Acknowledgements

We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “[evil Internet meme](https://cr.yp.to/papers/safecurves-20240809.pdf)” and the “[Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen](https://sockpuppet.org/blog/2015/08/04/is-extended-random-malicious/)” with good humor. Also thanks to [Filippo Valsorda](https://filippo.io/) for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.

    return int(datetime.fromisoformat(when).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())

def candidate(t, n, per, shift, width):

In our data set: only**208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts**, and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.

Our findings suggest that**90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks**. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.

The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:

Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage bill

Adjusted probability of task coverage

Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale)

Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from[Eloundou et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.10130). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.

For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.

As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.

## Methodology in brief

To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling**18,797** tasks across all occupations.

Example — 6 of the 22 tasks O*NET associates with Lawyers

1.   1 Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts.
2.   2 Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations.
3.   3 Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses.
4.   4 Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents.
5.   5 Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation.
6.   6 Supervise legal assistants.

To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the[Benchmark Index](https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/benchmarks/) tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:

*   **Public Availability.**Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.
*   **Agentic Tasks.**Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.
*   **Economic Realism.**Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.
*   **Economic Diversity.**We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.
*   **Balanced Difficulty.**Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.

Following work by[Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01203v2), we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with[human expert tags](https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/methodology/#expert-review) on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.

To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with[Hatgis-Kessell et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05172)’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.

A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the[Methodology](https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/methodology/) tab.

## Limitations

Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.

We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).

By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.

Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the[Benchmark Index](https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/benchmarks/) tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

## Patterns in coverage

The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by [Eloundou et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.10130)), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.

But even after controlling for AI-exposure,**O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:**

Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage bill

Adjusted probability of task coverage

Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale)

Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from[Eloundou et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.10130). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.

After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:

Benchmark coverage by O*NET task importance within occupations

Adjusted probability of task coverage

O*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale)

Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from[Eloundou et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.10130). Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.

The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.

## Can O*NET + benchmarks tell us how good AI is at your job?

Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.

We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our [Benchmark Map](https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/#map) suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.

O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that _each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average_, we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.

As a first step, we

Title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio

URL Source: https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference

Markdown Content:
content type Featured highlight

[MLX](https://mlx-framework.org/) on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. [In a previous post](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/exploring-llms-mlx-m5), we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see [Figure 1](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure1)), well above average human reading speed.

Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.

Figure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens. Higher is better. We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers.

We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on [Mac Studio](https://www.apple.com/mac-studio/specs/), using the MLX LM package, as described in our [prior post](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/exploring-llms-mlx-m5#running--llms-on-apple-silicon). We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.

We evaluate three frontier-class models ([Table 1](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#table1)) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).

| Model | Total Parameters | Active Parameters | Native Precision | Evaluation Precision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Muse Spark Open | 816B | 42B | BF16 | NVFP4 |
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 128B | 128B | FP8 | FP8 |
| Qwen 3.8 | 27B | 27B | BF16 | BF16 |

Table 1: Language models used in this post. Models ship in various precision formats; we evaluate Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 in their native precision, and Muse Spark Open in 4-bit (NVFP4) precision.

Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with `mlx_lm.benchmark`. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:

```
mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1
```

A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.

Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in [Table 2](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#table2) and [Table 3](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#table3), respectively.

Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In [Figure 2](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure2), we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.

Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see [Figure 2](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure2)). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.

Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see [Figure 3](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure3)), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.

Figure 2: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. The M5 Ultra GPU Neural Accelerator shines on compute-bound workloads.

Figure 3: Decode speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, and the M5 Ultra’s 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth (vs 819 GB/s on the M3 Ultra) is a key advantage.

The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see [Figure 4](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure4)): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.

Figure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra.

While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see [Figure 5](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure5)) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.

Figure 5: MLX supports two approaches to splitting large models across multiple computers. With pipeline parallelization, a model is split across depth, while with tensor parallelization, a model is split across width.

MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the [MLX distributed documentation](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/usage/distributed.html). These rely on fast inter-machine communication: [macOS 26.2](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-26_2-release-notes) introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (`jaccl`, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that `jaccl` uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides `mlx.launch`, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:

```
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline
```

In this command, `--backend jaccl` specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The `--env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1` flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).

In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see [Figure 7](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure7)) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.

It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see [Figure 6](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure6)). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by `--prefill-step-size 8192`) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk $k$, the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk $k + 1$, so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.

Figure 6: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Splitting the context (here into 8,192-token chunks) lets MLX overlap computation across the two machines — hence the speedup at 65,536 but not 8,192.

Figure 7: Decode speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Pipeline parallelization leaves decode speed essentially unchanged.

Tensor parallelization (see [Figure 5](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference#figure5)) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. articles.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
articles.content:
Title: How the Claude Code team does code review

URL Source: https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/

Published Time: 2026-10-15

Markdown Content:
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

## RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW

When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about [2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) this year.

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

Code review does two jobs:

1.   Find and fix issues before they ship
2.   Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed _when_ review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

## THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

## THE LIFE OF A CHANGE

A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

The life of a change

A typical Claude Code change, from the author's machine to users

**FIG A**Most of the path is automated; a person's attention goes where the risk is

## LAYER BY LAYER

Layers, not one gate

Six layers of checks, with rollback under them

**FIG B**Each layer catches some problems and misses others. Few get through all of them, and rollback handles the rest.

### 1. The work is verified before anyone else looks

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our [best-practices guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices).

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work [probably the most important thing](https://x.com/bcherny/status/2007179861115511237) for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

**When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source:** in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

*   `CLAUDE.md` tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.
*   `REVIEW.md`, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

### 2. AI review on every pull request

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, [Code Review for Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review), is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and `/code-review` runs a lighter version locally.

When we [launched the research preview](https://claude.com/resources/articles/code-review), the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

**Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them.** Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

**Every finding has to be answered.** You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

### 3. Security review that can block

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the `/security-review` command. Setup is covered in [automated security reviews in Claude Code](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11932705-automated-security-reviews-in-claude-code).

### 4. Automated checks that block

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume [here](https://claude.com/resources/articles/agentic-coding-is-straining-ci-heres-how-we-scaled-test-impact-analysis-at-anthropic).) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

### 5. Human approval, scaled by risk

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

| Risk | Examples | Human approvals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flag | None required once automated review and security checks are green |
| Medium | Ordinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system prompts | One person |
| High | The highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two people | Two people |

**The change sets the tier, not the author.** A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.

**Only trusted authors get the lighter paths.** Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

**Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it.** On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.

**An approval covers one specific commit.** If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.

### 6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the `latest` channel first. The `stable` channel trails it.

### 7. Fast detection, fast rollback

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.

## HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTER

Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop.

**Any incidents are now an eval.** The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.

Our incidents are the eval

Built from past incidents and reverts, run every day

**FIG C**The eval grows with every incident, and every change to the reviewer is scored against all of it.

**We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments.** It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how t

## TL;DR

*   StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood War
*   Each LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots
*   StarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot

The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates [StarSkirmish Bench v0.1](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-1/) with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness.

An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots.

### StarSkirmish Bench v0.2

1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots.

Gemini 4 Argon runs at `high`, the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at `max`.

GPT-6 Astra is the top scoring StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 LLM, a clear step ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol in second. Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 are functionally tied behind them, all scoring between 37 and 39.

### StarSkirmish Bench vs. Cost

StarSkirmish Bench score against the average API cost of one 1 hour run. Cost is on a log scale.

Muse Wonder Full's pricing is based on Muse Wonder's API pricing.

GPT-6.1 Sol offers uniquely good value: it is the only LLM in the most attractive quadrant, scoring second at just over a tenth of GPT-6 Astra's cost per run.

## [No Signs of Saturating](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#no-signs-of-saturating)

The strongest human written bots are still well ahead of every model. Against Stardust, PurpleWave and BananaBrain, the best model, GPT-6 Astra, wins only 7% of its games.

### Win rates vs the top human written bots

1 hour reasoning limits are a factor, but these matches are played on three 2 player maps. Real human written bot tournament conditions are significantly harder.

## [New AI Model Highlights](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#new-ai-model-highlights)

Google and Meta's new flagships replace v0.1's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3: Gemini 4 Argon places 3rd, and Muse Wonder Full 7th. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were covered in [v0.1](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-1/#model-breakdown).

*   Gemini 4 Argon uniquely preferred writing bots via one shots. Its five runs had the fewest builds and code versions of all the traced runs.
*   41% of its practice games were against high tier opponents, second only to GPT-6 Astra, yet its bots win only 7% of their games against those tiers, to Astra's 28%.

Favorite Strategy Timing Attack

## [AI Model Behaviors](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#ai-model-behaviors)

Each run's agent trace records how it spent its hour. The strongest predictor of a model's score is how much it practiced against the 7 strongest bots on the roster.

### Win Rates vs. Practice Against Strong Bots

StarSkirmish Bench score against the number of practice games a model's median run played against the 7 strongest roster bots during the hour. The dashed line is a linear fit across the 9 models.

GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon start playing these bots early in the hour, while their own bots still lose to them. Muse Wonder Full, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna rarely or never do. Claude Fable 5.1 is the outlier: it scores 37 while practicing almost entirely against weaker bots.

### Run-to-Run Variance

Results also vary between runs of the same model. Gemini 4 Argon varies far more than the other labs' flagships: its best and worst runs are 18 points apart, against 9 for GPT-6 Astra and 8 for Claude Opus 5.5.

## [Implementation Details](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#implementation-details)

## [Objective](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#objective)

Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against [BWAPI 4.4.0](https://github.com/bwapi/bwapi), played on [OpenBW](https://github.com/OpenBW/openbw). Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the [BASIL](https://www.basil-ladder.net/ranking.html) ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins.

The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling.

The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave).

## [Tournament Setup](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#tournament-setup)

45 LLM bots

13 Opponents

10,530 Games

18 Games / pair

Each model's 5 final bots play each of the 13 roster bots, the 10 competitive human written bots and the 3 demo bots, 6 times on each map, on fresh seeds. Unlike v0.1, the LLM bots don't play each other.

## [Harness and Reasoning](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#v01-vs-v02)

[StarSkirmish Bench v0.1](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-1/) ran every model in the same harness at 'high' reasoning. v0.2 runs each model in its lab's 1st party CLI harness at the highest reasoning setting it offers.

### Harness

v0.1 ran every model in one neutral 3rd party harness; v0.2 runs each lab's models in its 1st party CLI harness. Both versions give each model 1 hour.

v0.1

CLI versions: Claude Code 2.1.296, Codex 0.162.1, Antigravity CLI 1.3.5 and Muse Code 1.4.7.

### Reasoning Effort

v0.1 ran every model at high reasoning effort; v0.2 runs them at max.

v0.1

_Low_ _Medium_ _High_ _XHigh_ _Max_

Gemini 4 Argon runs at `high`, the highest effort supported.

Every v0.2 harness compacts the model's context at about 250k tokens. When a conversation nears that point, the CLI condenses it and the model carries on. Codex, OpenAI's CLI, for example, gives the GPT models its default 272k token window and triggers compression once 90% filled.

The CLIs' web search and web fetch tools are turned off, and the agent has no other internet access. The CLI is installed before the clock starts, and the hour counts from when the agent starts. There is no submit tool: the harness collects the bot when the time runs out.

## [Scoring](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#scoring)

v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its 234 tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won).

Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field.

## [Benchmark Correlations](https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/#correlations)

StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here.

### Benchmark Correlation

Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit.

Vals IOI ρ 0.95

WeirdML v3 ρ 1.00, n = 7

WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing.

One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.

Title: GitHub - cobanov/PS5LM: llama.cpp on a jailbroken PS5: run any GGUF model natively on the console, starting with Qwen 3.8

URL Source: https://github.com/cobanov/PS5LM

Markdown Content:
**Your PS5 runs the language model. Every device on your network uses it.**
 llama.cpp on the console's GPU, with OpenAI and Anthropic APIs and a screen made for the TV.

**[Get the app](https://github.com/cobanov/PS5LM/releases/latest)** · [Website](https://ps5lm.cobanov.dev/) · [Get started](https://github.com/cobanov/PS5LM#try-it) · [Issues](https://github.com/cobanov/PS5LM/issues)

> **New: decision models, powered by [Ollaya](https://ollaya.dev/).** PS5LM now runs Jev-like decision models (d1, Clef, OpenJev and more) on the GPU and answers the same `/v1/systemone` API as Ollaya: typed decisions with calibrated probabilities, in a fraction of a second.

PS5LM is for anyone with a jailbroken PS5 who wants a private model server at home. It loads a GGUF model onto the console's GPU and serves it to your laptop, your phone and your coding tools. It needs no PC while it runs, no cloud and no account.

Qwen 3.5 9B answering requests from a laptop on a PS5 Slim. Click for the video.

Home, Models, Console, API and Settings on the TV.

## A model server under your TV

*   **It runs on the GPU.** llama.cpp's Vulkan backend on the console's RDNA 2 GPU, with 11.4 GB of the shared memory for the model and its context. Every architecture and quantization llama.cpp knows comes along.
*   **It answers your network.** OpenAI's `/v1/chat/completions`, Anthropic's `/v1/messages` (Claude Code works against it) and a chat page in any browser. Point a client at `http://<console>:8081` and use any model name: the loaded one answers.
*   **It decides, too.** Load a decision model and the console answers TypeSafe's `/v1/systemone`: choice, score and yes-or-no questions about text and images, the API Ollaya serves on a PC.
*   **It shows its work.** Every request streams across the TV as a chat: which device asked, what it asked, and the reply as it is written. Square sends a demo and Triangle opens a keyboard, so the console can be tried from the couch.
*   **It watches the console.** A Console page charts temperature, power, GPU and CPU load over the last two minutes or the last hour, beside a table of every reading.
*   **It picks what fits.** The planner reads each GGUF and gives it the longest context and best cache that fit the memory free. A Suggested list holds models measured on the console, and the app downloads from Hugging Face by itself, to internal storage, the M.2 drive or a USB drive.
*   **It reads images.** Models with an image projector (Gemma 4, MiniCPM-V, d1) take pictures in chat and in decisions.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen 3.5 0.8B, Q4_K_M | 0.5 GB | 207 tokens a second |

| Qwen 3.8 27B, UD-Q2_K_XL | 9.2 GB | about 20 tokens a second, 64k context |

[Ollaya](https://github.com/ollaya-dev/ollaya) runs open decision models on a PC the way Ollama runs language models. PS5LM brings the same idea to the console: a decision model reads a state and answers typed questions in one forward pass, with no text generated.

 "intent": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "What does the customer want?",

 }
}'

The Suggested list has d1 Omni 600M, d1 3B and Clef Flash. Any GGUF that carries llama.cpp's decision metadata loads the same way, and the app labels it a decision model.

You need a PS5 on firmware 7.00 to 13.60, jailbroken, with these payloads loaded:

articles.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
articles.content:
Title: You could have invented transformers from memory

URL Source: https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/

Published Time: 2026-10-15

Markdown Content:
Retrieving a character from memory. The recall worsens as the number of memories grows.

Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And _how much can they store?_

In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

* * *

The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they _interfere_ with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its **capacity**.

We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A **memory store** is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A **memory** is one key-value pair: a **key** $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a **value** $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we **query** it with an input $x$, and it **recalls** an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an _associative memory_.

## An outer product memory store[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#an-outer-product-memory-store)

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

$$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$

where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$.[1](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#fn:1)1 Sometimes this accumulation of keys and values is called “Hebbian learning”, since the strength of the synapses (weights) is increased by inputs (keys) and outputs (values) that fire together (are correlated).

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights.[2](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#fn:2)2 This outer-product memory store is used for the state of linear attention, also called fast weights: each token stores the memory $(k, v)$ by adding $v k\transpose$ to a matrix that later tokens query ([Katharopoulos et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16236); [Schlag, Irie & Schmidhuber](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11174)).

Aside: a gradient descent step writes a memory
Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is

$$W \leftarrow W - \eta\, \bar y x\transpose.$$
This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see [Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05798), who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.

To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:

$$f(x) = V\transpose K x = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,(k_i\transpose x).$$

So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.

### Recall picks up interference[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#recall-picks-up-interference)

So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?

Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then

$$f(k_j) = \underbrace{v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} v_i\,(k_i\transpose k_j)}_{\text{interference}},$$

meaning we get back the value of the **target memory**, the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and

$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \sim \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k}}.$$

Setting this ratio to 1 gives a capacity of

$$M \approx d_k,$$

once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.

stored memories _M_ = 32

the target memory each other stored memory, weight relative to the target memory

interference / signal = 0.64 recall fails

## How do we reduce interference?[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#how-do-we-reduce-interference)

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall.[3](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#fn:3)3 This is for recalling a clean value vector. If each value only needs to point toward the right answer among a fixed set, like selecting the most likely token, a recall just has to land closer to the right answer than to the wrong ones, and a $d\times d$ matrix can hold about $d^2$ facts ([Nichani, Lee & Bietti](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06538)). To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to _reduce interference_.

The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we’ll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.

## The optimal linear memory store[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#the-optimal-linear-memory-store)

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem:[4](https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/#fn:4)4 We can also use this regression objective to design short-term memories that a sequence model writes during the forward pass, like linear attention and self-attention. See [my work on test-time regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12352).

$$\operatorname*{minimize}_W \sum_{i=1}^M \norm{W k_i - v_i}_2^2.$$

When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is

$$W = \parens*{\sum_i v_i k_i\transpose}\parens*{\sum_i k_i k_i\transpose}\inverse = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse.$$

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys’ covariance $K\transpose K$. This _whitens_ the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren’t orthogonal.

When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes

$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k} - 1}.$$

This ratio equals 1 at

$$M = 2d_k,$$

so the optimal store’s capacity is _twice_ as large as before!

Aside: deriving the optimal linear memory store
**When $M \leq d_k$.** If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and

$$W = V\transpose (KK\transpose)\inverse K$$
fits every memory exactly. When $M < d_k$, the problem is underconstrained and has infinitely many solutions, and this one is the min-norm solution. The rows $\tilde k_i\transpose$ of $(KK\transpose)\inverse K$ are known as the dual basis for the rows of $K$: by construction, $(KK\transpose)\inverse KK\transpose = I$, so $\tilde k_i\transpose k_j = \delta_{ij}$. Then $f(k_j) = \sum_i v_i\, \tilde k_i\transpose k_j = v_j$, so there is _no interference_ and we have perfect recall.

**When $M > d_k$.** Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$. Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.

Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$. For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:

$$f(k_j) = \sum_{i=1}^M v_i\, P_{ij} = \underbrace{P_{jj}\, v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} P_{ij}\, v_i}_{\text{interference}}.$$
$P$ is the projection onto the column space of $K$, a $d_k$-dimensional subspace of $\reals^M$. Two facts about projections help us analyze the interference-to-signal ratio:

*   **The signal term:** By the cyclic property of the trace, $$\sum_{j=1}^M P_{jj} = \trace{K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose} = \trace{(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpo
